items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) In a revision session, a student says: “The control group in Hölzel et al.’s study did not receive any MBSR training during the study period.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Describe the procedure of Hölzel et al.’s study.
items.answer: (a) Correct. They were on a waiting list and offered the course afterwards. (b) Healthy adults with no meditation experience took an 8-week MBSR course (weekly 2.5-hour sessions, a retreat day and home practice); MRI scans were taken before and after, as for a waiting-list control group, and grey matter concentration was compared.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2] (b) 1 mark MBSR course; 1 mark MRI before/after; 1 mark control group comparison [3]

items.stem: Explain the difference between a target population and a sample.
items.answer: The target population is the whole group the researcher wants to generalise to; the sample is the smaller group selected from it who actually take part.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each definition, contrasted [2]

items.stem: A therapist in Seoul is treating Grace, a teenager with a fear of cockroaches that involves strong disgust. Explain one reason why a treatment that worked for the boy in Saavedra and Silverman’s case may not work for Grace.
items.answer: The boy was a single case with a unique history; Grace’s phobia may have a different cause, and individual differences mean responses to treatment vary.
items.markingKey: 1 mark single case; 1 mark individual differences [2]

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that Milgram’s study should not have been carried out? In your answer, you may refer to usefulness and deception.
items.answer: Arguments for: Participants suffered extreme stress, including seizures, and were deceived. The prods undermined the right to withdraw. Arguments against: The findings are important for understanding atrocities such as the Holocaust. Participants were debriefed and most were glad to have taken part. Milgram could not predict the levels of distress. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: accurate, detailed psychological knowledge (named studies/theories) used to build a two-sided argument; evaluation includes issues such as validity, reliability, generalisability, ethics or usefulness; a justified conclusion. Middle band: relevant knowledge with some evaluation, but one side or the conclusion is underdeveloped. Lower band: limited, mostly descriptive answer with little evaluation.

items.stem: Sipho replicated Andrade’s study in Bangkok. 8 participants shaded shapes while listening to a boring telephone message and 8 participants just listened. All then had a surprise test of the names and places mentioned (out of 16). Table: Names and places recalled (out of 16) — Doodling: 8, 7, 8, 7, 8, 4, 9, 10. Control (no doodling): 8, 7, 6, 5, 5, 6, 7, 8. (a) Name a suitable type of graph to display the mean scores for the two conditions, and justify your choice. (b) The participants were people who replied to an advertisement on a community website in Bangkok. Identify the sampling technique used and explain one weakness of it.
items.answer: (a) Bar chart, because the IV has separate (discrete) categories, so the mean for each condition is shown as a separate bar with gaps between bars. (b) Volunteer sampling. Weakness: volunteers may share characteristics (for example being more curious or helpful), so the sample is self-selected and may not represent the target population.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: bar chart; 1 mark: justification (discrete conditions / categories, not continuous data) [2] (b) 1 mark: sampling technique; 1 mark: weakness explained [2]

items.stem: “Pozzulo et al.’s (2009) study of children’s and adults’ line-up identifications has more strengths than weaknesses.” Evaluate this view, including usefulness in your answer.
items.answer: Strength (usefulness): The findings can inform how police conduct line-ups with child witnesses, for example by warning that the culprit may not be present or using procedures that reduce pressure to choose. Strength (standardisation): All participants saw the same stimuli and were tested with the same line-up procedure and instructions, so children’s and adults’ performance could be compared fairly. Weakness (generalisability): The children were a narrow age range from one area, so the results may not apply to older children or to children from other cultures. Weakness (ethics): Children cannot give fully informed consent, so parental consent was needed, and children may feel anxious about being “wrong”. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: strengths and weaknesses are accurate, well explained and clearly linked to the study, the named issue is discussed, the answer is well organised and reaches a conclusion. Middle band: points are mostly accurate but one side is less developed or links to the study are general. Lower band: points are identified but brief, generic or one-sided. Description of the procedure without evaluation receives little credit.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) In a revision session, a student says: “Piliavin et al.’s findings can be generalised to all countries and all time periods.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain one way Piliavin et al.’s study lacked control.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. The study took place in New York in the late 1960s; norms about helping vary across cultures and over time. items.stem: Mateo wants to find out whether young children prefer toys associated with their own gender. Plan an observation to investigate this. Your plan must include: how inter-rater reliability will be checked, ethical issues and behavioural categories.
items.answer: Method: an observation. Variables: IV: gender of the child; DV: time spent playing with each toy. Sample: for example an opportunity or volunteer sample of about 30 people from the target population in Manila, with reasons. Design/procedure: clear, replicable steps, with standardised instructions and random allocation or counterbalancing where relevant. Ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, protection from harm, confidentiality and a full debrief. Data: quantitative scores summarised with means and a suitable graph; qualitative answers analysed into themes where collected.

Top band: a detailed, accurate and replicable plan using the stated method; all required features are included and are appropriate to the aim; variables are operationalised; ethics are addressed. Middle band: a workable plan with most required features but some lack detail or are not justified. Lower band: a basic plan with few features or with errors in method.

items.stem: ‘Phobias are best explained by classical conditioning.’ To what extent do you agree?
items.answer: Arguments for: The button phobia began after a single unpleasant event when buttons fell on the boy, consistent with conditioning. Exposure therapy based on conditioning reduced his fear. Arguments against: Not everyone who has a bad experience develops a phobia, so individual factors matter. Disgust, a cognitive and emotional response, had to be treated separately. Biological preparedness may explain why some fears develop more easily. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.

items.stem: ‘Validity is more important than reliability in psychological research.’ Discuss this view.
items.answer: Arguments for: A consistent but inaccurate measure is useless. Ecologically valid studies such as Piliavin et al. tell us about real behaviour. Arguments against: Without reliability, results cannot be checked or trusted. Standardised laboratory procedures (for example Milgram) allow replication. Both are needed and are linked. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.

items.stem: Evaluate Fagen et al.’s (2014) study of elephant learning, including a discussion of ecological validity.
items.answer: Strength (usefulness): The trunk wash allows elephants to be tested for tuberculosis safely, and the method shows mahouts an effective, humane alternative to traditional training. Strength (ecological validity): Training took place in the elephants’ normal environment with their own mahouts, so the behaviour was learned in real working conditions. Weakness (controls): There was no control group trained with traditional methods, so we cannot be sure positive reinforcement was more effective than other methods. Weakness (reliability): Each elephant had a different mahout and individual temperament, so the procedure was not identical for all animals and may be hard to replicate exactly. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

Top band: strengths and weaknesses are accurate, well explained and clearly linked to the study, the named issue is discussed, the answer is well organised and reaches a conclusion. Middle band: points are mostly accurate but one side is less developed or links to the study are general. Lower band: points are identified but brief, generic or one-sided. Description of the procedure without evaluation receives little credit.
